meta.title: Visit Barbizon — Cultural Cartography
meta.description: A cultural guide to Barbizon, the painters' village on the edge of the Fontainebleau forest: studios, museums, trails and places to eat and stay, on one map.

why.title: Where art history meets the forest.
why.p1: In the nineteenth century, painters left Paris and settled in this small village at the edge of the Fontainebleau forest. Working outdoors, they studied weather, light and ordinary rural life, laying the groundwork for modern landscape painting.
why.p2: Today Barbizon is still a place of thresholds: between studio and path, stone and sand, village street and forest clearing. Visit Barbizon traces these crossings rather than listing attractions.

map.body: See how studios, paths and clearings relate to one another on a layered map of the village and the forest edge.

park.title: Where to park
park.body: Public parking sits just off the Grande Rue and near the forest entrance. From there, most of the village is reachable on foot within a few minutes.

start.title: Where to start
start.body: Begin with a slow walk along the Grande Rue, then visit one small museum or studio before turning toward the forest paths.

bestTime.title: Best time to visit
bestTime.body: Early mornings and late afternoons offer softer light and quieter paths, especially outside high-summer weekends.

about.title: Barbizon, map in hand
about.p1: Visit Barbizon is a guide to the village, built around a map. It brings together places, stories and walks, from the village centre to the edge of the Forest of Fontainebleau.
about.p2: Barbizon is where painters learned to look at the forest. The site shows the village one layer at a time: art and history; shops, restaurants and places to stay; the forest; practical information. Everything is on a single map, for you to explore at your own pace.
about.p3: Places are checked on the ground, and our own photographs are taken on the spot. Historical details are checked against archives, and the sources are listed on the {{historyLink}} page. Everything is written in French and English.
about.p4: Visit Barbizon was created by Luigi Pérez, who lives and works in Barbizon.
about.p5: New places and stories are added over time. Spotted a mistake or have a suggestion? Write to {{email}}.
about.closing: Visit Barbizon is powered by Civitas Layers.

meta.title: History — Visit Barbizon
meta.description: Historical postcards, a visual timeline and the sources behind the project: two centuries in the painters' village.

history.title: A village, a forest, and two centuries of looking.
history.intro: Alongside contemporary photographs and maps, Visit Barbizon draws on historical postcards, guidebooks and archival images. The village has been looked at and described for nearly two centuries. This page gathers some of those ways of seeing, and traces the events that shaped what there is to see.

corot1822.headline: Corot paints in the Fontainebleau forest.
corot1822.detail: Camille Corot makes his first studies in the Fontainebleau forest. Other landscape painters follow, and the practice of working on the motif, outdoors, takes hold. Barbizon, a simple hamlet at the forest edge, soon becomes their base.

aubergeGanne.headline: The Auberge Ganne, the painters' home.
aubergeGanne.detail: François Ganne and his wife run a grocery on the Grande Rue that serves drink and food, then takes in lodgers. From the 1820s to the 1860s, painters stay there; they decorate the furniture, the panels and even the bedroom walls. The inn becomes the home of what will be called the Barbizon School.

denecourt1842.headline: Denecourt marks the first trails.
denecourt1842.detail: A former sergeant of the Empire who became the "Sylvain" of Fontainebleau, Claude-François Denecourt begins in 1842 to lay out trails marked with blue arrows, often described as the first waymarked walking trails in the world. He opens about 150 kilometres of them and publishes guides for walkers. Many of today's routes still follow his paths.

rousseau1847.headline: Théodore Rousseau settles in Barbizon.
rousseau1847.detail: Rousseau rents a house on the Grande Rue and sets up his studio in the adjoining barn; he will spend the last twenty years of his life there. Refused by the Salon for more than a decade, he is readmitted after the Revolution of 1848, which also brings him a state commission.

millet1849.headline: Jean-François Millet arrives with his family.
millet1849.detail: Millet leaves Paris in 1849, the year of the cholera epidemic. His house on the Grande Rue remains his studio until his death: there he paints The Sower, The Gleaners and The Angelus.

reserve1861.headline: An "artistic reserve" protects the forest.
reserve1861.detail: After years of campaigning, led notably by Rousseau and the painters, a decree of 13 August 1861 withdraws 1,097 hectares of the Fontainebleau forest from logging on the grounds of their artistic value. It is often described as the first nature reserve in the world. The argument was aesthetic: this landscape deserved protection because painters had taught people how to see it.

rousseauDeath.headline: Death of Théodore Rousseau.
rousseauDeath.detail: Rousseau dies in Barbizon in December 1867. He is buried in the Chailly-en-Bière cemetery: Barbizon is then only a hamlet of that commune.

milletDeath.headline: Death of Millet; Barbizon becomes a place of pilgrimage.
milletDeath.detail: Millet dies in January 1875 and is buried beside Rousseau in the Chailly cemetery; Corot dies a few weeks later. The founding generation passes, but interest in Barbizon does not fade: a new kind of cultural tourism takes root.

commune1903.headline: Barbizon becomes a commune.
commune1903.detail: Until then a hamlet of Chailly-en-Bière, Barbizon becomes a commune in its own right in 1903. The village gains its independence, and soon its own cemetery.

musee1995.headline: The Auberge Ganne becomes a museum.
musee1995.detail: Bought by the commune in 1987, the old inn is restored. The works uncover, on the upper floor beneath old wallpaper and whitewash, the sketches and studies the painters left on the walls. The museum opens in 1995; the Seine-et-Marne Département takes over its management in 2004.

today.headline: Same scale, same street, same forest edge.
today.detail: Barbizon is still one long street between open farmland and the forest. What drew the painters here, the light, the sense of a threshold, the closeness of the wild, is largely intact.

painters.title: The people who came to look.
painters.intro: Between 1830 and 1875, hundreds of painters and sculptors, French and foreign, stayed in Barbizon. Here are a few of them.
painters.corot: Painted in the Fontainebleau forest from the 1820s, and showed the others the way.
painters.rousseau: Settled permanently in 1847. De facto leader of the school.
painters.millet: Settled in Barbizon in 1849. Stayed until his death.
painters.diaz: One of the founding figures of the school. A plaque on the Grande Rue recalls his time here.
painters.jacque: Painter and etcher, he arrived with Millet in 1849. He kept poultry and planted the village's first asparagus.
painters.daubigny: Came to Barbizon from 1843, before settling at Auvers-sur-Oise. A plaque marks the house he lived in.
painters.troyon: A friend of Rousseau and Dupré, he worked with them at Barbizon in the 1840s.
painters.dupre: Rousseau's friend from the 1830s, he painted alongside him at Barbizon in the 1840s.
painters.barye: An animal sculptor, he also painted the gorges of Franchard and Apremont in the late 1840s, alongside Millet and Díaz.
painters.bodmer: Swiss painter and etcher, settled in Barbizon around 1849. The oak that bears his name stood in the Bas-Bréau.
painters.hunt: American painter and friend of Millet, he bought the 1850 Sower, now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
painters.monet: In 1865 he painted the Bodmer oak, in the Bas-Bréau woods.
painters.ziem: Known for his views of Venice, he also came to Barbizon, where a plaque commemorates him.

sources.title: Where this comes from.
sources.p1: Historical content on this platform is checked against institutional and period sources: Base Mérimée / POP, the Archives de Seine-et-Marne (including the Chailly-en-Bière censuses), Gallica / BnF and the nineteenth-century press, the Barbizon town hall's map and publications, and museum records. Local archival research by grappilles.fr informs many narratives and is credited as a valued contribution.
sources.p2: Factual accuracy is a core principle of this project. A date, name or place is published once it has been checked against at least one documentary source, or against direct local knowledge. Checking continues page by page, and corrections are welcome: info@explorebarbizon.com.
sources.p3: Local village knowledge is further informed by Barbizon, le Guide, a blog by Jean-Michel Mahenc, former president of the Barbizon Tourism Office, covering village life, restaurants, boutiques and trails. Like grappilles.fr, it is treated as a research lead: anything we publish is checked against the sources above.
